source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) The Structure-Mapping Engine: algorithm and examples
finding: SME output has three parts: correspondences, candidate inferences, and a structural score. Candidate inferences are new expressions that the match suggests are true in the target. They are surmises, not valid conclusions.
numbers: Three outputs per mapping (gmap). Example gmap #1 (water flow to heat flow) has weight 6.99 and one candidate inference: CAUSE(>TEMPERATURE, HFLOW).
quote: Each candidate inference must be interpreted as a surmise, rather than a logically valid conclusion.
limits: SME has no knowledge of either domain and no logic built in. Validity testing is explicitly left to other modules.
agent_relevance: Direct model for O7: the mapping step produces conjectures, and a separate check (code or test) must accept or reject each one.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) The Structure-Mapping Engine: algorithm and examples
finding: A base statement can be carried over only if two conditions hold: it is consistent with the mapping's substitutions, and it is structurally grounded, meaning part of it already matches the mapping. Statements unconnected to the matched structure are not inferred.
numbers: Algorithm: for each base root that is an ancestor of a matched root in the gmap, every descendant not yet in the gmap becomes a candidate inference. Cost: worst case about O(N^2), typical about O(N); with one gmap and no missing structure, constant time.
limits: Grounding is purely syntactic. A fact can be grounded and still be false in the target.
agent_relevance: Rule for the agent: only transfer a source fact that hangs off a relation already mapped. Ungrounded transfers (surface-similar facts) are the main error source.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) The Structure-Mapping Engine: algorithm and examples
finding: Worked example: GREATER-THAN(DIAMETER(coffee), DIAMETER(ice-cube)) is NOT a candidate inference of the pressure-to-temperature mapping, because it does not connect to the mapped causal structure. Only the CAUSE link between temperature difference and heat flow is projected.
numbers: Fig. 7: three gmaps. #1 weight 6.99 (pressure/temperature/flow, 1 candidate inference), #2 weight 3.94 (diameter, 0 inferences), #3 weight 2.44 (liquid, flat-top, 0 inferences).
limits: One worked physical example; not a human-subject test.
agent_relevance: Shows systematicity acting as an inference filter: the best-scoring mapping is also the one that yields the useful inference.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) The Structure-Mapping Engine: algorithm and examples
finding: When a base entity has no target partner, SME adds a hypothetical target entity as a skolem function of the base entity. In the heat-flow case this produced an unknown conjectured entity, (:skolem pipe), which a later module resolved to physical contact or immersion.
numbers: Second heat-flow analogy was almost entirely candidate inferences, since the system had no prior model of heat flow (a carryover analogy: model built by analogy rather than augmented by it).
limits: Skolem entities are placeholders; the engine cannot say what they are.
agent_relevance: The agent can record 'unknown X plays role of source Y' as an explicit open slot, then fill it by search or test, instead of inventing a filler.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) The Structure-Mapping Engine: algorithm and examples
finding: SME's only built-in consistency check on inferences is weak and structural: it discards a candidate inference if the predicate is non-commutative and its arguments are just a permuted copy of an existing target expression.
numbers: Example: if GREATER(MASS sun, MASS planet) is in the target, GREATER(MASS planet, MASS sun) is dropped.
limits: Catches direct contradictions of a known kind only. It does not catch causal or domain-level contradictions.
agent_relevance: A cheap code-level check for O7 (reject a transferred claim that contradicts a known target fact) and shows how thin the original check was.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) The Structure-Mapping Engine: algorithm and examples
finding: The authors contrast SME with Holyoak's pragmatic account: relevance to the goal drives retrieval and mapping. They say this has no account of soundness through systematicity, only works in problem-solving contexts, and ignores that access follows surface similarity.
numbers: Three stated limits of the pragmatic model. SME paper also states a tuning idea: a conservative strategy might favor gmaps with some candidate inferences but not too many, to raise the chance of being correct.
limits: Authors' own framing of a rival theory; the rival (ACME, Holyoak and Thagard 1989) was not opened this session (UCLA host refused connection).
agent_relevance: Our agent has a goal (a problem to solve), so a goal-driven filter on which facts to transfer is legitimate; but structure alone should gate what is allowed.

source: Clement & Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping
finding: Experiment 1: when people judge which matching facts belong to an analogy, they prefer a fact embedded in a shared causal system over an equally good match that is not embedded. The control group (target story only) shows no such preference.
numbers: N=48 undergraduates. Choice task: analogy subjects chose the shared-system fact 67% to 92% of the time across four passages; target-only controls 42% to 54%. Ratings: shared-system M=6.28 vs different-system M=4.89 for analogy group; controls 5.22 vs 5.31. Interaction F(1,44)=13.99, p<.001.
limits: Fisher tests significant for 3 of 4 passages. Short artificial science passages; written stimuli.
agent_relevance: Evidence that the human inference filter is relational systems, not isolated similarity. Supports requiring the transferred fact to be tied to a mapped causal chain.

source: Clement & Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping
finding: Experiment 2: the central candidate-inference test. Key facts were removed from the target. Subjects predicted new target facts from the analogy. They mostly predicted the fact whose causal antecedent matched the base (the shared-system fact), not an equally plausible fact whose antecedent did not match.
numbers: N=32 (16 analogy, 16 target-only). Free prediction: shared-system .53, different-system .12, other .27 (analogy group); target-only .12, .12, .74. Ratings: 6.03 vs 4.41. Choice score: M=2.9 vs 1.8 of 4, F(1,28)=16.43, p<.001.
limits: Only for two passages did analogy and control groups differ significantly in choice; one passage may have been biased toward the shared-system fact. Mostly one analogical depth.
agent_relevance: Primary human evidence that inference projection follows systematicity. The agent should rank candidate inferences by how deep they sit in matched structure.

source: Clement & Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping
finding: Experiment 3 repeated Experiment 2 with new materials and found the same pattern, plus a clear measure: shared-system minus different-system predictions per subject.
numbers: N=48 (24 analogy, 24 target-only). Mean (shared minus different) predicted: analogy .92 vs target-only .13, F(1,44)=5.15, p<.05.
limits: Effect smaller in some passages; within-paper replication by the same lab.
agent_relevance: Moderately robust within one lab; independent replication is needed (see later angles).

source: Clement & Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping
finding: Written justifications show why: analogy subjects explained their chosen inference by pointing to the matching causal structure. The authors argue relations are matched by their role in a larger system, even when low-level relations differ.
numbers: Explanations coded into four categories in Experiments 1 and 2 (counts in paper tables, not recorded here).
limits: Justification text is post hoc; consistent with our guardrail that reasoning text is not evidence (G10).
agent_relevance: Supports having the agent state the mapped relation chain that licenses each inference, but check it by code, not by trusting the story.

source: Bartha / Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Analogy and Analogical Reasoning
finding: Bartha's articulation model judges an analogical inference with two tests: Prior Association (the source's known similarities are tied to the projected feature by a clear link) and Potential for Generalization (that same link plausibly holds in the target, with no critical disanalogy).
numbers: Qualitative criteria; no numbers.
limits: The article says the model may be vague or too permissive. Based on advocate-and-critic dialogue.
agent_relevance: A usable O7 check: (1) name the source link, (2) look for a target feature that breaks the link. This is a counterexample search.

source: Bartha / Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Analogy and Analogical Reasoning
finding: Hesse's three conditions: material similarities, causal vertical relations in the source, no essential difference between source and target. Norton's material theory: no universal form; each analogical inference is licensed by a local fact about the domain.
numbers: Qualitative.
limits: Review calls Hesse too narrow (formal analogies, correlation-only cases like Franklin's lightning) and says 'essential' depends on the use. Norton's theory fails when the uniformity is what the inference is trying to show.
agent_relevance: Warns that a general rule for valid analogy does not exist; the agent needs domain checks, not a universal scorer.

source: Bartha / Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Analogy and Analogical Reasoning
finding: Determination-rule account (Davies and Russell): an analogical inference is valid if the property is a function of some factors P1..Pm and source and target agree on all of them. The source stays essential.
numbers: Used-car example in the review.
limits: You need a justified determination rule; the problem of justification returns as the problem of justifying the rule.
agent_relevance: Shows when analogy becomes deduction: if we can state and test the rule, we should test it directly.

source: Bartha / Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Analogy and Analogical Reasoning
finding: Systematicity does not guarantee a good inference. The review's example (Antarctica to Mars): the more systematic mapping gave the weaker inference, because freezing temperatures act as preventive causes.
numbers: One worked example.
limits: Single philosophical counterexample, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Do not use a structural score as a proxy for truth. Keep an independent test (G3).

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat college students on text analogy tasks, including letter-string rule transfer, which is analogical inference (apply a source change to a new target).
numbers: Digit matrices: N=40 humans; GPT-3 above humans (generative OR 95% CI 1.21 to 2.91; multiple choice OR=6.27, p=2.3e-8). Letter strings: N=57 humans, GPT-3 better overall (OR=1.76, p=6.3e-5). Story analogies: N=54 humans; GPT-3 above chance but below humans (OR=0.37, p=0.0003); 15 of 54 humans were perfect.
limits: Letter-string problems are on the web (the authors admit this in review). GPT-3 was weaker at choosing the analogous story when the match was causal and cross-domain (far).
agent_relevance: Base-rate: a plain LLM already does simple relational transfer; the scaffold should not add a step there. Hard cases are far domain and causal.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-4 (preliminary) was stronger on the story analogy task, picking the analogous story even in the far (cross-domain) condition and near perfect in the near condition.
numbers: Reported in Supplementary Fig. 6; no exact value in the main text.
limits: Preliminary only, and the task uses Gentner et al. 1993 materials, so contamination is possible.
agent_relevance: Model strength on far analogy rose with scale, so distant-source use (O7) may get cheaper over time.

source: Hodel & West (2023/2024) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Failed generalization: with a permuted alphabet and larger step size, GPT-3 and GPT-4 degrade, and the authors argue the original problems may be in the training data so zero-shot is unproven.
numbers: They also had ChatGPT list letter-string examples, taken as a sign of exposure. A human behavioural experiment in the appendix agrees with Mitchell's critique.
limits: Authors say membership in training data cannot be proved; the ChatGPT probe is circumstantial. Webb et al. reply that GPT-4 with code execution fixes the problem.
agent_relevance: Do not trust an LLM's analogy score on a familiar puzzle form. Test on mutated or counterfactual variants.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Counterfactual letter-string analogies (shuffled alphabets, symbols) cut GPT accuracy sharply while humans stayed high. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 were not better than GPT-3 overall.
numbers: Over all alphabets and problem types: humans .753 (1,876 samples), GPT-3 .488, GPT-3.5 .350, GPT-4 .452 (6,840 samples each). Error mix, wrong rule: 30.97% GPT-3, 32.67% GPT-4, 14.67% humans.
limits: Humans scored higher here than in Webb et al.; protocol differences. A counting/indexing problem may explain part of the drop (next line).
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that transfer by pattern fit is brittle; supports G3: test the inference on a variant not seen.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Reply to both critiques: the failures on shuffled alphabets come from counting letter positions. GPT-4 with code execution solved the counterfactual problems at about human level without being told to use code.
numbers: Human N=99 on the shuffled-alphabet task. 46% of GPT-4's errors followed a valid alternative rule vs 39% of errors in the human data from Lewis and Mitchell. Interval size 2 was harder for humans (P=1.5e-11) and GPT-4 (P<2e-16) but not significant for GPT-4+code (P=0.066).
limits: Code execution is not a human-like route; supports a tool-use view, not a pure reasoning view. Exact accuracy values were in figures, not read.
agent_relevance: Hint for the agent: where an inference needs exact indexing or counting, route the step to code, not to the model.

source: Stevenson, Pafford, van der Maas, Mitchell (2025) Can LLMs generalize analogy solving like children can?
finding: Children (7 to 9) and adults transfer a letter-string rule to Greek and symbol alphabets with no loss. LLMs lose accuracy as the alphabet gets less familiar.
numbers: Proportion correct Latin/Greek/Symbol: adults .88/.91/.89 (n=62); children .62/.66/.67 (n=41); GPT-4o .85/.63/.48; Claude-3.5 .68/.62/.46; Llama-3.1 405B .79/.74/.27; Gemma-2 27B .60/.39/.14 (54 runs each).
limits: Zero-shot, one task family. Models tested with the best of five prompt templates.
agent_relevance: Same lesson: rule carry-over in LLMs depends on familiarity. Keep the novel-domain case as a stress test.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024, ICLR) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Analogical prompting: the model first writes related problems and their solutions, then solves the target. It beat 0-shot and few-shot CoT on average in GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces and BIG-Bench with GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4 and PaLM 2.
numbers: Average gain about +4% over baselines (abstract). Codeforces Acc@1: GPT-3.5-turbo with the method 15% vs GPT-4 16%. K=5 self-generated examples for GSM8K, K=3 for MATH and BIG-Bench.
limits: Self-generated examples fail on weak models: with text-curie-001 and davinci-001, retrieved few-shot beat it. It needs more output tokens. Table cell alignment is garbled in my text copy; per-model cells not recorded.
agent_relevance: The main direct LLM test of source-to-target carry-over by prompt. The source is generated by the same model, so G4 and G7 apply: check it against plain CoT at equal tokens.

source: Sourati, Ilievski, Sommerauer, Jiang (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives
finding: On narrative analogies built from Gentner's near/far and surface/system distinctions, LLMs are far below humans, especially for far analogies. GPT-4 is below chance on far analogies when distractors are near.
numbers: Zero-shot averages: models 57% vs humans 96% (50% random). Near analogies: humans 97.9%, models 75.0%. Far analogies: humans 94.1%, models 39.6% on average (below chance).
limits: Task is identifying the analogy, not carrying a fact over. Binary choice format.
agent_relevance: Far-domain source selection is the weak point; reinforces keeping O7 to impasse use.

source: Jiayang et al. (2023) StoryAnalogy: deriving story-level analogies from LLMs
finding: 24K story pairs annotated with entity and relation similarity from extended structure-mapping theory. Multiple-choice analogy identification is hard for LLMs.
numbers: ChatGPT about 30% accuracy vs humans 85.7%, random 25%. Annotator agreement (Fleiss kappa) moderate: 47% entity, 42% relation similarity, on 1K sampled items.
limits: Crowd annotation, moderate agreement. A fine-tuned FlanT5-xxl matched zero-shot ChatGPT on analogy generation.
agent_relevance: Judging relational similarity is noisy for models and for annotators; treat model-made mappings as unverified.

source: Bhavya, Xiong, Zhai (2022) Analogy generation by prompting LLMs: InstructGPT
finding: InstructGPT can generate source analogies for a target concept; the largest model reached human-level quality on that task, but explaining why two concepts are analogous remains weaker. Prompt wording matters.
numbers: 1.4K generated analogies human-rated. Best prompts were short imperative statements at low temperature. Biggest quality gain from 0.3B to 1.3B parameters (19.17% and 15.34% relative).
limits: Quality rated as meaningful or not, not verified as inference-valid. Sensitive to spelling errors and prompt form.
agent_relevance: LLMs can supply sources cheaply; the open weakness is verification of the transfer, which is our O7 check.

source: Sultan & Shahaf (2023) Life is a circus and we are the clowns: finding analogies between situations and processes
finding: Pipeline to find and map analogies between natural-language procedural texts without hand-written logic, because classic SME-style inputs need human-built representations.
numbers: Used as a baseline in StoryAnalogy: about 44.9% in a multiple-choice table (random 25%); row read from a partly garbled table.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction of this paper were read.
agent_relevance: Shows the feasibility of text-to-structure mapping; the representation bottleneck that limited SME is partly removed by LLMs.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) The Structure-Mapping Engine
finding: SME uses only match rules plus structural consistency (one-to-one, parallel connectivity); flexibility lies in swappable rules. The authors state that tuning for human data had not been needed so far.
numbers: Matching steps are polynomial, typically bounded by O(N) per stage.
limits: Authors flag tailorability risk: hand-translating stimuli into formal form may leak the answer. The algorithm does not address it.
agent_relevance: The representation step decides inference quality; in our agent that is S2, and it should be code-checked.
